801: D is correct because encrypting the data at the company's data center before uploading it to S3 is client-side encryption, which keeps the encryption keys entirely outside the AWS Cloud and satisfies the requirement to manage keys externally. The data remains encrypted in transit to S3 and at rest because the ciphertext is what gets stored in the bucket. The server-side encryption options keep keys within AWS services such as AWS KMS or S3, which violates the external key management requirement.
802: D is correct because Amazon API Gateway provides a fully managed HTTP endpoint for mobile devices to submit payment notifications, and AWS Lambda performs the basic validation before passing notifications downstream without any infrastructure to manage. The long-running backend runs on Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type, a serverless compute option that lets the company adjust CPU and memory per task while AWS manages the underlying infrastructure. This combination meets all requirements with the least operational overhead.
803: A is correct because Amazon Cognito user pools provide managed, highly scalable authentication that supports millions of users. Cognito's risk-based adaptive authentication evaluates signals such as unusual geographical locations, IP addresses, and devices, and automatically invokes MFA only when a login appears risky, which matches the conditional two-factor requirement exactly. The alternatives are not designed for risk-aware authentication at consumer scale.
804: C is correct because AWS Glue is a serverless ETL service that can run the daily transformation job and load the data without provisioning or managing any infrastructure. Amazon Redshift Serverless is a fully managed data warehouse with massively parallel processing that scales automatically, and Amazon Redshift ML lets data analysts create and train machine learning models directly with SQL commands. Together they satisfy the serverless, MPP, and SQL-based ML requirements.
805: C is correct because an AWS Outposts rack is AWS-managed physical infrastructure installed in the company's own data center, delivering native AWS managed services such as Amazon EKS and Amazon EC2 locally while all data remains on-premises for compliance. The company can use EKS and other AWS managed services without any data leaving the data center. Data transfer or edge appliances do not host the full set of AWS managed services.
806: B is correct because an AWS Storage Gateway S3 File Gateway presents an NFS file share to the existing on-premises workloads while transparently storing the data in Amazon S3, eliminating the scaling limits of the local NFS datastore. An S3 Lifecycle policy can then transition the stored data to lower-cost storage classes, making this the most cost-effective migration path. Volume Gateway provides block storage instead of the required NFS interface, and EFS options do not address the on-premises migration as cost-effectively.
807: D is correct because provisioned concurrency keeps a pool of Lambda execution environments initialized and warm, eliminating cold starts so service latency is maintained during high-concurrency marketing events. Increasing the memory setting also proportionally increases CPU and network allocation, and following AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations right-sizes each function so CPU-intensive code completes faster; since Lambda charges by duration, faster execution reduces compute costs. Reducing memory would slow execution and raise costs, and reserved concurrency only caps concurrency rather than preventing cold starts.
808: A is correct because Amazon ECR is the native private image repository for ECS task definitions, and enabling scan-on-push with the ECR basic scan automatically checks every pushed image, including newly created images, for CVEs with no changes to the workloads. It is the simplest fully managed way to achieve continuous vulnerability scanning for existing and future container images. The other options require storing images outside ECR or migrating workloads to EKS, adding unnecessary complexity.
809: A is correct because an Amazon EventBridge rule can match the AWS Batch job state change event for SUCCEEDED, and an EventBridge API destination is the native serverless way to invoke a third-party HTTP API, supporting basic authentication with a username and password stored in the connection. This requires no compute resources, delivering a fully serverless solution. EventBridge Scheduler is time-based rather than event-based, and routing through API Gateway and Lambda adds unnecessary overhead.
810: C is correct because AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity between VPCs across separate AWS accounts without requiring an internet gateway, VPN, or Direct Connect connection. The vendor places a Network Load Balancer in front of the RDS for MySQL database and exposes it as a VPC endpoint service, and the company creates an interface endpoint in its VPC to reach the database entirely over the private AWS network. This is the only workable option given the absence of any existing network connectivity between the two environments.
811: B is correct because creating the Amazon Managed Grafana workspace inside a VPC allows Grafana to reach data sources through private internal networking. Creating a private endpoint for the Amazon RDS database keeps all database traffic on the AWS private network, so the data is never exposed to the internet. Configuring that private endpoint as the Grafana data source therefore satisfies the security requirement.
812: C is correct because AWS Glue DataBrew is a prebuilt, no-code data preparation service that analysts use to visually define transformation steps such as filtering anomalies, normalizing date and time values, and generating aggregates. DataBrew also provides data profiling and data lineage, and its recipes can be shared and reused so employees throughout the company can apply the same transformation steps. It is the only option that meets the no-code, lineage, and sharing requirements without writing scripts or SQL.
813: A is correct because an A record for the development website pointing to the ALB keeps the DNS configuration stable, while an ALB listener rule matches requests for the development hostname and forwards them to the target group containing the single development instance. If the development instance is replaced, the new instance is simply registered in the same target group and traffic routes to it automatically without any DNS changes. This satisfies the requirement to route automatically to the development instance even after replacement.
814: B is correct because Amazon EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane, allowing the containerized Kubernetes application to migrate to AWS with minimal refactoring. Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service based on ActiveMQ that supports the AMQP protocol the application already uses, preserving the existing messaging behavior. Migrating to ECS or Lambda would require refactoring away from Kubernetes, and SQS does not support AMQP.
815: D is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses AWS edge locations and the AWS global network backbone to route user traffic over an optimized path to the NLB endpoints in each Region, reducing end-to-end load time for a global customer base. A standard accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and continuously reroutes traffic to the closest healthy Region endpoint, improving both performance and availability. Simply load balancing with Route 53 or adding Regions does not optimize the network path itself.
816: B is correct because AWS Transfer Family provides a fully managed SFTP server endpoint that is natively integrated with Amazon S3, so vendors with legacy SFTP-based applications can continue uploading files exactly as before while the data lands in S3. The company manages no servers or infrastructure, which gives the least operational overhead. Self-managed SFTP on EC2 or gateway-based alternatives require significantly more administration.
817: C is correct because Amazon Textract extracts text and insights from the PDF news reports, and Amazon Comprehend is a fully managed NLP service that analyzes the extracted text for content and sentiment without building or training any model. Saving the analysis to an S3 bucket is simple and adds no operational burden. Both services are serverless, making this the lowest-overhead solution that satisfies the requirement to use Textract.
818: A is correct because Amazon Kinesis data streams provide scalable real-time ingestion of data from third-party applications, and Kinesis Data Firehose can consume those streams and reliably deliver the raw data to the specified S3 bucket destination. This is the standard serverless pipeline for real-time ingestion into Amazon S3. The other options do not provide real-time streaming ingestion into S3.
819: B is correct because DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so the established pattern of storing large payloads as objects in Amazon S3 and keeping a pointer attribute with the S3 URL in the DynamoDB item is the most operationally efficient way to handle large and growing data. It leverages S3's virtually unlimited object size while DynamoDB continues to serve the primary application data. No extra Lambda functions, compression logic, or item-splitting logic is required.
820: C is correct because Amazon EventBridge Scheduler supports recurring schedules at scale for hundreds of jobs, and running the containerized cron jobs on AWS Fargate requires no refactoring of the job code and no infrastructure to manage. EventBridge Scheduler also supports one-time schedules, so jobs can be run at a specific future event time. This meets the requirements for minimal refactoring, managed scheduling, and future event-based execution.
